one_liner: Rust web server and reverse proxy with automatic TLS and built-in tracing; markets nginx-class speed but publishes no numbers.
what_it_does: Ferron is a standalone HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 server for static files, reverse proxying with load balancing, FastCGI/SCGI/CGI, caching and automatic ACME certificates, configured through its own compact ferron.conf syntax. It is not a drop-in for nginx: the configuration language differs (a from-nginx migration page exists), and features are compiled-in modules. Version 3 (default branch develop-3.x) is still a release candidate (3.0.0-rc.9); Ferron 2 is the stable and LTS line.
how_it_is_fast: Ferron 3 runs on zincio, the project's own thread-per-core async runtime (one primary thread per CPU core, io_uring on Linux when the io_uring directive is turned on, otherwise epoll via mio), with zincio-http's in-house HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 stacks and splice-based zero-copy sending for HTTP/1.x static responses. TLS is rustls (aws-lc-rs provider for QUIC and the proxy client), the Unix build links jemalloc, and the release profile uses LTO with codegen-units=1 and panic=abort. The cross-build scripts offer an optional PGO build trained with wrk/h2load scenarios, which the project says gives 10-20%; no measurement backs that figure.
when_to_use: Small to mid-size sites and API gateways that want automatic TLS and a short config file without tuning, where nginx-level throughput is enough rather than required to be beaten.
Debugging-heavy deployments: per-request traces linked to logs, OTLP, Prometheus and StatsD export are built in.
Teams that want a memory-safe (Rust) replacement for a Caddy- or nginx-style front server and can run release-candidate software.
Mixed workloads on one box: static files, reverse proxy with round-robin and keep-alive upstreams, PHP through FastCGI.
when_not_to_use: When you need a measured speed win over nginx: no benchmark data, hardware or results are published in any repository, and an HN commenter who ran reverse-proxy tests found Ferron roughly on par with nginx.

Security-sensitive edges before 3.0 final: seven advisories were published on 2026-09-25, including a critical auth_to fail-open with proxy, an HTTP/2 Rapid Reset variant in the in-house HTTP/2 stack and an unauthenticated HTTP/3 SETTINGS CPU DoS.
Existing nginx configurations with complex location logic, Lua or third-party modules: there is no config compatibility.
Production that needs a stable major release: 3.x is still rc.9 and its runtime has changed between major versions (tokio and hyper in 1.x, Monoio in 2.x per HN comments, zincio in 3.x).

integration.form: standalone server binary (Rust workspace; modules compiled in, custom builds possible)
integration.dependencies: zincio and zincio-http (own runtime and HTTP stack), tokio, hyper 1 (proxy client), rustls 0.23 with aws-lc-rs, quinn (QUIC), async-compression (zstd, brotli, gzip), tikv-jemallocator on Unix, mimalloc on Windows; git submodules opentelemetry-proto and phc-winner-argon2
integration.min_toolchain: Rust stable via rustup, edition 2021; no rust-version or rust-toolchain file in the repository
integration.platforms: Linux (cross-build targets x86_64, i686, aarch64, armv7, riscv64, s390x, ppc64le; glibc and musl), Windows (IOCP, Windows service), macOS/BSD via mio
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (server); multi-threaded data plane with one primary thread per CPU core by default, set by the cpu_affinity directive
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: serves the same roles as nginx (static files, reverse proxy, TLS termination) but needs a rewritten configuration

gotchas: Harness behind ferron.sh/benchmarks (ferronweb/benchmarking, 3 commits on 2026-09-02) builds nginx from unpinned master with plain ./auto/configure, so nginx gets its default -O (i.e. -O1) plus -g with no --with-cc-opt, while Ferron gets LTO, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort; every server is built from an unpinned branch and no results, hardware or versions are committed.

The 'static files with Zstd compression' scenario does not compress with the committed client: client/benchmark.py runs h2load with no -H option and h2load sends no Accept-Encoding, so both servers serve identity responses; if the header is added by hand (as the server README's manual example does), nginx compresses at level 3 and Ferron at a hard-coded level 4 with window_log 17 and hash_log 10, and medium.bin is 2 MB of random, incompressible bytes.

Charts history: the 2025 reverse-proxy chart left nginx out 'due to possible misconfiguration'; in issue #185 the maintainer said nginx lacked upstream keepalive and later called his rerun's nginx numbers possibly unreliable; nginx was only added to the static charts in January 2026. The sweep's req/s counts every completed stream including non-2xx (h2load req_success), with errors only in a separate CSV column.

io_uring is off by default (the benchmark configs do not enable it), compression levels are fixed at 4 for every algorithm, and the static compressor treats .bin and other unknown extensions as compressible.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Ferron over Caddy (the other batteries-included server here, also without a verified win over nginx) when you want Rust memory safety and built-in request tracing and can accept release-candidate status; if you need numbers showing a win over nginx, the measured siblings routez (1.19-1.26x reported) or rproxy are better-evidenced, though they are narrower proxies rather than full servers.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing has been measured that can be checked: the README says only 'fast and consistent under load', the website charts (ferron.sh, unreachable here) come from an unpinned h2load-over-HTTPS/2 harness with no committed results or hardware, and the only third-party statement (HN, snippet only) puts Ferron near nginx as a reverse proxy.
status_note: Very active (commits to 2026-10-10, 3.0.0-rc.9 on 2026-10-04, 2.2k stars, MIT) and usable today via the stable 2.x LTS line, but the 3.x line is a release candidate that just shipped seven security fixes and has no reproducible performance evidence.
